newsitem.title: UK: Major tells Conservatives to fight to keep power.
newsitem.headline: Major tells Conservatives to fight to keep power.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major set the seal on Friday on a rousing pre-election conference by urging his ruling Conservative Party to close ranks and fight for a fifth consecutive term of office.

Major, exuding confidence after pro- and anti-European factions agreed to bury the hatchet for the sake of party unity, hammered home the need for harmony in the few months that remain to the election, which be held by May.
"The well-being of the Conservative Party is more important than any member of it," Major said in his closing address.

"So the lesson is clear, Everyone in the Conservative Party should work -- and if I know them, will work -- heart and soul, irrespective of personal interests, to secure the re-election of a Conservative government," he added.
Labour, in opposition since 1979, led the Conservatives by around 20 percentage points in opinion polls before this week's conference.
But the race is expected to tighten after a series of passionate appeals for unity from cabinet heavy-hitters, giving Major a fighting chance of winning the Conservatives an unprecedented fifth term.
"It's been the week the Tory family came together -- to renew the family contract with the British nation," he said.

In what aides billed as a personal statement aimed at capitalising on Major's image as the trusted "man next door", the prime minister painted Labour as a party of opportunists with no firm principles.

The Conservatives, by contrast, could offer a proven track record of enhancing "opportunity for all" through its commitment to lower taxes and reforming the welfare state to create "a self-help society -- not a help-yourself society".
"At this election there's a central question. It's this: who can be trusted with the future?" the prime minster asked.

To prove that the Conservatives had opportunity in "the bloodstream of our party", Major recapped a list of initiatives that his ministers had outlined during the week and added some They included a pledge to continue spending more on the health service year in, year out, and plans for the electronic tagging of persistent juvenile defenders as young as 10 years old to keep them from making mischief on the streets.
On the vexed issue of Europe, Major said the only realistic future was for the European Union to develop as a flexible and responsive partnership of nations, not a United States of Europe.
In tough language on Northern Ireland, he condemned the Irish Republican Army for a bomb attack on Monday on Britain's main army base in the province, which killed one soldier.
No one would take Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, seriously until they showed a serious commitment to end violence for good, Major said.

"I promise the people of Northern Ireland this: for as long as there is a political breath in my body, I will fight for a secure way of life in Northern Ireland and for a settlement fair to all," he said.
